generalizedRange: High mountains of Central and South Asia
hook: The ghost of the mountains is real — and almost never seen.

story.text: Herders call it the ghost of the mountains. Against grey rock, its smoky, rosetted coat makes it all but invisible even to a trained observer.
Everything about it is built for cold stone: the densest fur of any big cat, wide fur-lined paws, and a tail nearly as long as its body, wrapped on for warmth in sleep.
Its world is broken terrain — cliffs, outcrops, ravines — across twelve countries, at altitudes where summers reach eighteen thousand feet.
A single cat may need up to a thousand square kilometers of this emptiness to live.
Most snow leopards killed by people die in retaliation for attacks on livestock, or to prevent them.
Poaching and declining wild prey press from one side; a warming climate presses from the other, reaching these mountains at twice the hemisphere's average rate.
The hopeful work is coexistence: predator-proof corrals that keep herds safe at night, and herder cooperatives whose wool income rises when the cats stay alive.
For all its power, the cat is not known to be aggressive toward humans.
To witness the snow leopard is to keep attention on an animal built to escape it.
Its future rests on choices made far below the snowline — how herds are guarded, how wool is sold, how warming is slowed.

reproduction.text: Mating runs from January into late March; two cubs is the usual litter, born after a gestation of around a hundred days. The mother raises them entirely alone, and they stay with her for up to twenty-two months learning the mountains.

insight.text: A snow leopard cannot roar. It chuffs and purrs — and can pounce as far as six times its own body length.

programs.title: Snow Leopard Enterprises
programs.summary: Over 400 herder women in 40 communities sell handmade wool goods, raising income up to 40% while their communities pledge to protect the cats.

programs.title: Snow Leopard Program
programs.summary: Surveys populations, trains national biologists, and builds predator-proof corrals that protect about 25 snow leopards a year in Ladakh.
